title: Round-Trip PnL from a Trade Blotter

statement.md: A trading desk hands you a one-day blotter for a **single instrument**: $N$ fills, each tagged `B` (buy) or `S` (sell) with a quantity and an execution price carrying exactly two decimal places. The trader opens the day flat, never goes short, and closes flat — every unit bought is eventually sold — so the day's realized PnL is simply total sale proceeds minus total purchase cost:

statement.tex: \text{PnL} = \sum_{\text{sell fills}} q \cdot p \; - \; \sum_{\text{buy fills}} q \cdot p

statement.md: The catch is **money arithmetic**. A price like `10.10` is not represented exactly in binary floating point, and summing tens of thousands of products as floats can drift the final cent. The pattern used by real back-office systems is to convert each price to **integer cents** once, accumulate everything in integers, and only format a decimal string at the very end.

statement.title: Cents, not floats
statement.md: As a double, `0.01` is really 0.01000000000000000020816… — harmless for one trade, dangerous when compounded over a whole blotter. Integer cents make money arithmetic exact and language-independent.
Print the total PnL in dollars with exactly two decimals, with a leading minus sign for a losing day.

inputFormat:
Line 1: integer $N$ — the number of fills.
Lines 2 to $N+1$: `B q p` or `S q p` — side, integer quantity $q$, price $p$ with **exactly two decimal digits**.
outputFormat: One line: the day's total PnL with exactly two decimal places (for example `12.00`, `-29.00` or `0.00`).
constraints: 0.01 <= p <= 1000.00, always written with exactly two decimal digits
The running position never goes negative and ends at exactly 0
Total money movement fits in a signed 64-bit integer
hints: Convert each price to integer cents by parsing the string: `w.dd` becomes `w * 100 + dd`.
Keep one signed integer accumulator in cents; subtract buys, add sells.
Format from the integer at the end: dollars = abs(cents) // 100, remainder = abs(cents) % 100 zero-padded to two digits.

editorial.md: Because the trader starts flat, never goes short, and ends flat, every bought unit is sold exactly once. Cash-wise each `B q p` line pays out $q \cdot p$ and each `S q p` line takes in $q \cdot p$, so the net cash change over the day — the realized PnL — is the signed sum of the fill values.

Parse each price as the decimal string it is: `w.dd` maps to integer cents `w * 100 + dd`. Multiply by quantity, accumulate into one signed 64-bit counter, and convert to a `dollars.cents` string only when printing. With the given limits the accumulator's magnitude stays near $10^{14}$ cents — far inside 64-bit range.

editorial.title: Two classic bugs
editorial.md: Accumulating `qty * price` as doubles can be off by a cent after many fills; and rounding a float at print time can turn a `x.xx5` value into the wrong cent. Doing everything in integer cents kills both bugs at once.

solutions.python:
import sys

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().decode().split()
    n = int(data[0])
    cents = 0
    i = 1
    for _ in range(n):
        side = data[i]
        q = int(data[i + 1])
        whole, frac = data[i + 2].split('.')
        price_cents = int(whole) * 100 + int(frac)
        i += 3
        if side == 'B':
            cents -= q * price_cents
        else:
            cents += q * price_cents
    sign = '-' if cents < 0 else ''
    a = abs(cents)
    sys.stdout.write(f"{sign}{a // 100}.{a % 100:02d}\n")

main()
